passage: Thomas had four hours to submit a market report to a client in Nairobi, and the office printer and half the network were down. He used an AI writing tool to draft the summary from his data. It was fast and fluent. His colleague Pallavi glanced at it. "That growth figure looks odd." Thomas checked: the tool had made up a number that wasn't in his data. His stomach dropped. With the clock ticking, he went through every figure, line by line, against the spreadsheet. Two more were wrong. He fixed them and added a note that AI had helped draft the text but he had verified the numbers. He sent it with twenty minutes to spare. He told Pallavi, "I owe you tea."

qa.q: What did the AI tool make up in the report?
qa.a: It made up a growth figure that wasn't in his data.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when he found the made-up number?
qa.a: He felt a jolt of fear, as his stomach dropped, realising he'd almost sent false data.

qa.q: What did Thomas do right under time pressure?
qa.a: He checked every figure against the spreadsheet, fixed errors and was open about using AI while staying responsible for the numbers.

qa.q: What would have happened if Pallavi hadn't glanced at the report?
qa.a: The client might have received false figures, damaging trust in Thomas and his firm.

grounding: Shows a young professional using AI under pressure while verifying results and keeping accountability.

passage: Sahil, a junior developer at a Pune software firm, had started using an AI assistant to write most of his code. His team lead, Pankaj, noticed Sahil's pull requests getting bigger and faster. One afternoon Pankaj asked him to explain a function line by line. Sahil couldn't. His ears went red. "The AI wrote it," he mumbled. Pankaj didn't scold him. "Use it, it's useful. But if you can't explain it, you can't own it." They agreed that Sahil would write core logic himself each Friday, and use AI for tests and boilerplate. He would also review every AI suggestion before committing. After a month, Sahil caught an AI bug in someone else's code during review. He felt proud.

qa.q: On which day would Sahil write core logic himself?
qa.a: He would write it himself each Friday.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when he couldn't explain the function?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed; his ears went red and he mumbled his answer.

qa.q: What balance did Sahil and Pankaj agree on?
qa.a: Sahil would use AI for tests and boilerplate, write core logic himself on Fridays and review every AI suggestion.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see the AI assistant?
qa.a: He sees it as a useful tool but insists the developer must understand and own the code it produces. 👍

grounding: Shows a young developer learning to delegate to AI while keeping accountability and protecting his own skills.

qa.q: What would change if Hansa printed the newsletter unchecked?

passage: Last spring our firm brought in an AI tool to summarise contracts, and I loved it. What used to take me a morning took twenty minutes. By summer I had stopped reading the full documents at all. Then my senior, Mridul, asked, 'Eshaan, what does the indemnity clause say?' It was in a supplier contract I had 'reviewed'. The summary had skipped it. I hadn't read it. I remember the silence on that call. Nothing bad had happened yet, but it could have, and my name was on the review, not the tool's. Since then I use the summary as a map, not the territory: I read every clause it flags and spot-check the ones it doesn't. Once a week I review one contract fully by hand, so I don't lose the skill. Mridul calls it my gym day. I'm slower than I was in summer. I'm also better.

qa.q: What did the AI summary skip?
qa.a: An indemnity clause in a supplier contract.

qa.q: What did Eshaan feel during the silence on that call?
qa.a: Embarrassed and alarmed, realising Eshaan's name was on a review that had not really been done.

qa.q: How does Eshaan now use the tool responsibly?
qa.a: Eshaan treats summaries as a map, reads the flagged clauses, spot-checks the rest, and reviews one contract fully by hand each week to keep the skill.

qa.q: How might Mridul see Eshaan's weekly 'gym day'?
qa.a: As a sensible habit that keeps the junior sharp and accountable, which is why Mridul jokes about it approvingly.

grounding: A young professional looks back on over-relying on an AI tool and how they now verify its work and protect their own skills.

passage:
Supervisor's note, customer-support pilot (Uday, operations head):
Pallavi, 24, led our trial of an AI assistant for routine customer queries. What stood out was not the speed, though replies went from hours to minutes. It was her caution. Before launch she tested it on two hundred real past queries and found it confidently gave wrong refund rules in about one in ten. She refused to go live until those were fixed. She insisted that every complaint, refund or angry message goes to a human, and that each reply says it came from an assistant. She also kept two team members answering some queries by hand every day, 'so we don't forget how'. One week an agent flagged a wrong answer anyway; Pallavi traced it and shared the fix openly. Next step: I have asked her to write our guidelines for any future AI tools.

qa.q: How many past queries did Pallavi test the assistant on?
qa.a: Two hundred real past queries.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's refusal to go live suggest about what she cared about?
qa.a: She cared more about customers getting correct answers than about launching quickly or showing off speed.

qa.q: Which of Pallavi's safeguards keep humans accountable?
qa.a: Sending complaints, refunds and angry messages to people, labelling assistant replies, keeping staff practising by hand, and tracing errors openly.

qa.q: How does Uday see Pallavi's work?
qa.a: He values her caution over speed and trusts her enough to ask her to write guidelines for future tools.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a young employee deploying an AI assistant responsibly with human oversight and verification.

passage:
Thursday night
Nearly a disaster today. I used the drafting assistant to write the research section of the brief for Rukmini Ma'am, the senior partner. It cited four judgments. They looked perfect. At 5 p.m. she asked me to pull the full text of the third one. I couldn't find it anywhere. Because it didn't exist. The tool had invented it.
She didn't shout. She asked, "Did you read them?" I said no. Worst feeling of my year.
We fixed it by nine: I found two real judgments that actually said what we needed. She said, "Use the tool to find leads. You're still the lawyer."
New rules for me: every citation, I open and read. And once a week I'll research one question fully by hand, so I don't forget how.
— Amandeep

qa.q: How many judgments did the assistant cite?
qa.a: Four judgments.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when Rukmini Ma'am asked 'Did you read them?'
qa.a: Amandeep felt deeply ashamed, calling it the worst feeling of the year.

qa.q: Which of Amandeep's new rules protect both accuracy and skill?
qa.a: Opening and reading every citation, and researching one question fully by hand each week so the skill isn't lost.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Ma'am see the incident?
qa.a: She treats it as a serious but teachable mistake, staying calm and making clear that accountability stays with the lawyer.

grounding: A young associate's diary shows an AI tool inventing a legal citation, and new rules for verification and keeping skills.

passage: The new phone app promised to identify crop disease from a single photo, and the agriculture department had asked Chetan, the young extension officer, to use it in the villages around Solapur. At Sonali's pomegranate orchard he photographed a spotted leaf. The app said "bacterial blight, 94 percent" and suggested a spray. Sonali, who had farmed these trees for nine years, frowned. "Blight spots look different. These came after the hailstorm." Chetan hesitated. It would be easy to trust the screen. But if the spray was wrong, Sonali would lose money and the soil would take the chemicals for nothing. He took three samples to the district lab instead. The result came back a week later: hail damage, no disease. Chetan wrote to the department suggesting that every app result be checked by an officer or lab before any spray was advised. Sonali sent him a box of pomegranates.

qa.q: How long had Sonali farmed the trees?
qa.a: Nine years.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when the app and Sonali disagreed?
qa.a: Chetan felt uncertain and tempted to trust the screen, but uneasy about the cost of being wrong.

qa.q: How did Chetan keep accountability while using the app?
qa.a: He treated its answer as a lead, sent samples to the district lab, and proposed that every app result be checked before a spray is advised.

qa.q: How might Sonali see the app after this?
qa.a: Sonali probably sees it as a tool that can be wrong, and feels respected that her experience was taken seriously.

grounding: A young extension officer in rural Maharashtra checks an AI crop app's answer instead of passing it on blindly.

passage:
In the logistics office in Ho Chi Minh City, Nadia's desk faced the river, but she rarely looked at it. Her job was the weekly shipping report, and for three months the company's AI assistant had drafted it for her in ten minutes.

On Thursday, she noticed the container count for Da Nang looked high. The assistant had counted a cancelled shipment twice. The report had already gone to her manager, Bao, in draft.

Her stomach dropped. She went straight to his desk. "The draft has an error. It's mine to fix, not the tool's. I didn't check the cancellations."

Bao nodded slowly. "Good that you caught it. What will you change?"

"I'll check every total against the booking system before sending. And once a month, I'll do the whole report by hand, so I don't forget how."

Bao smiled. "Write that down for the team. They're all using it."

qa.q: What did the AI assistant count twice?
qa.a: The assistant had counted a cancelled shipment twice.

qa.q: How did Nadia feel when she noticed the error?
qa.a: Nadia felt a jolt of alarm, her stomach dropped, but she also felt responsible and went straight to Bao.

qa.q: What steps did Nadia plan so this does not happen again?
qa.a: She will check every total against the booking system before sending and do the report by hand once a month to keep her skills.

qa.q: How might Bao see Nadia after she reported the error?
qa.a: Bao seems to trust her more, seeing that she takes responsibility, and he wants the team to learn from her checks.

grounding: A young employee owns an AI-drafted error, commits to verifying results and keeps doing the task by hand to avoid losing the skill.

passage:
The coaching institute's staffroom was quiet except for the photocopier when Yash dropped a stack of sheets on Suraj's desk.

"Question 7's answer key is wrong. Three students came to me."

Suraj's face went hot. He had used an AI tool to generate the whole practice set the night before and printed it without solving it himself.

"The tool made the question," he said, then stopped. "No. I put it in front of the students. I'm responsible."

"What will you tell them?"

"The truth. That I didn't check, and that the students who argued with the key were right." He was already writing on the board of the empty classroom next door.

That afternoon, in front of forty students, he explained the mistake and gave the three students credit for catching it.

Afterwards he set a rule for himself: the tool could draft questions, but he would solve every one before printing, and write at least a quarter of each set on his own.

qa.q: How many students came to Yash about question 7?
qa.a: Three students came to Yash.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when Yash pointed out the wrong key?
qa.a: Suraj felt embarrassed, his face went hot, and he was tempted for a moment to blame the tool.

qa.q: What rule did Suraj set, and why does it help?
qa.a: He will solve every AI-drafted question before printing and write at least a quarter himself, which checks accuracy and keeps his own skills sharp.

qa.q: How might the three students feel when Suraj credits them in class?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and respected, seeing that questioning a key was right and valued.

grounding: A young teacher who used AI to draft questions takes responsibility for an error and sets rules to verify and keep his own skill.

passage:
Subject: How we use the coding assistant (proposal)

Hi Divyansh and team,

After last week's outage, I've been thinking about how we use the AI coding assistant. To be clear: the bug was in code I approved. The assistant wrote it, but my name was on the review.

So here's what I'd like us to try from Monday:

1. Anything the assistant writes gets reviewed like a junior's code. No "it looks fine".
2. Every AI-generated function needs a test we write ourselves.
3. On Fridays, pick one small task and do it without the assistant. Divyansh, I know you'll groan. But I noticed I couldn't remember how to write a basic query last month, and that scared me.
4. If you're unsure whether the assistant's answer is right, ask a person.

Let's discuss at stand-up. Tell me if any of this feels unworkable.

Thanks,
Samir

qa.q: What happens on Fridays in Samir's proposal?
qa.a: On Fridays, the team picks one small task and does it without the assistant.

qa.q: What worried Samir enough to suggest the Friday rule?
qa.a: Samir felt scared on noticing an inability to remember how to write a basic query, a sign of skills slipping.

qa.q: What makes Samir's proposal responsible use of AI?
qa.a: It keeps human accountability for approved code, requires review and self-written tests, and protects skills with regular practice.

qa.q: How might Divyansh react to the proposal?
qa.a: Divyansh might groan at first about the Friday rule, but could appreciate that Samir owned the bug instead of blaming the tool.

grounding: A young team lead proposes rules for AI-assisted coding that keep accountability, verification and skills with the humans.

passage:
You asked, Mahima, what it's like leading the team that brought AI into our customer support. I'm Rekha, and the honest answer is: it's not the tool that's hard, it's staying responsible.
When we started, the AI answered customer emails directly. It was fast. Then one day it told a customer they'd get a full refund they weren't entitled to. Another day, it invented a delivery date. The customers were angry at us, not at the AI.
So we changed the rules. The AI drafts; a person approves anything about money, safety or promises. We check a random ten per cent of everything else every week. And every agent still handles some tickets fully by hand, so they don't forget how.
My boss asked who's accountable when it goes wrong. I said: me. The AI can't apologise to a customer. We can.

qa.q: What does the AI do now, according to Rekha's new rules?
qa.a: The AI drafts, and a person approves anything about money, safety or promises.

qa.q: How did Rekha seem to feel when the AI made mistakes?
qa.a: Rekha seemed alarmed and responsible, since the customers were angry at the team, not the AI.

qa.q: Which of Rekha's rules prevent skill atrophy, and why does that matter?
qa.a: Every agent still handles some tickets fully by hand, so they keep the skills needed to catch and fix the AI's errors.

qa.q: How might the customers see the new process?
qa.a: Customers would likely trust the company more, getting accurate answers with a human standing behind promises.

grounding: Shows a young team lead deploying AI while keeping human accountability, verification and skills.

passage:
I'm Jaya. I sit next to Kavitha on the data team, and I've watched how she works with AI.
She uses an AI assistant for first drafts of analysis code, like most of us. But she does something I didn't, at first. Before she trusts any number, she checks it a second way: a quick calculation by hand, or a small sample she can count herself. Twice I saw her catch errors that would've gone into client reports.
Once a week, she writes a small analysis entirely by herself, no AI. When I asked why, she shrugged. "If I stop, I won't notice when it's wrong."
She also writes a note in every report: which parts were AI-assisted and how she checked them.
I don't know if she worries about the tool. She seems calm about it. But when our manager asked who he could trust with the big client audit, he picked her.

qa.q: How often does Kavitha write an analysis entirely by herself?
qa.a: Once a week.

qa.q: What does Kavitha's "If I stop, I won't notice when it's wrong" suggest about her mindset?
qa.a: It suggests Kavitha feels cautious and responsible, determined not to lose the skill needed to judge the AI.

qa.q: Which of Kavitha's habits could Jaya adopt?
qa.a: Jaya could check AI numbers a second way, do regular work without AI, and note which parts were AI-assisted.

qa.q: Why did the manager pick Kavitha for the audit?
qa.a: The manager trusted her because her checking habits show she stays accountable for results.

grounding: Illustrates, through a colleague, a young analyst delegating to AI while verifying results and preventing skill loss.

passage:
Monday: Vidya, a junior associate at a Mumbai firm, used an AI tool to summarise a sixty-page supplier contract. It produced a neat one-page summary. She sent it to her manager, Simran.
Wednesday: Simran called her in. "The summary says we can cancel with thirty days' notice. Page forty-two says ninety." Vidya went red. She'd trusted the summary without checking the key clauses.
Simran didn't shout. "The tool saved you hours. But you signed the summary, so it's yours."
Friday: They agreed on a process. The AI drafts the summary; Vidya checks every number, date and obligation against the contract and marks the page. Once a month, she summarises one contract fully by hand, to keep her reading sharp.
The next summary took an hour longer. It was right.

qa.q: What notice period does page forty-two say?
qa.a: Ninety days.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel when Simran pointed out the error?
qa.a: Vidya felt embarrassed and caught out, going red because she hadn't checked the key clauses.

qa.q: What process did they agree, and why does it matter?
qa.a: AI drafts, Vidya checks each number, date and obligation against the contract and marks the page, and she practises by hand monthly, keeping accountability and skill.

qa.q: How might Simran see the extra hour on the next summary?
qa.a: Simran would likely see the extra hour as worth it, because an accurate summary protects the firm.

grounding: Shows over a week a young professional learning to delegate to AI while staying accountable and keeping skills.

passage: Sit down, Rehana, before you send that report. Let me tell you what happened when I was about your age, just after these AI tools arrived in our firm. I, Rajni, was the fastest analyst on the floor, and I let the assistant draft a whole market summary for a client. It read beautifully. I skimmed it, signed it, sent it. Two days later the client called. One statistic in it didn't exist anywhere; the tool had simply made it up. My director didn't shout. She asked, "Whose name is on the report?" Mine. Not the tool's. I was so ashamed I couldn't eat that evening. After that I made myself a rule: I check every number to its source, and once a month I write one analysis fully by hand, so I don't forget how. So, before you send yours, let's check the numbers together.

qa.q: What was wrong with the market summary?
